query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high‐entropy alloy, rapid dislocation activity during deformation (especially at lower temperatures and high strain rates) drives a transient but local enrichment of the principal elements at grain boundaries. When this kinetically induced segregation surpasses a critical threshold, the grain‐boundary cohesion degrades and brittle intergranular failure ensues. In contrast, under slower or higher-temperature deformation where diffusion can homogenize the composition, the same alloy retains ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase, compositionally complex HEA (for example, an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy) with no preexisting precipitates or engineered microstructural features.
generation.intervention: Subject equivalent samples to two different deformation protocols: (1) a rapid, low-temperature/high strain rate protocol designed to maximize dislocation density and minimize solute relaxation, and (2) a slower (or elevated temperature) deformation protocol where sufficient time is allowed for solute re‐distribution to prevent localized segregation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests performed in a service-relevant intermediate temperature range (e.g., around 500°C) under dynamic loading conditions; this ensures that the HEA remains single-phase yet has a chance for dislocation-driven segregation under rapid deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Local grain-boundary compositional fluctuations—specifically, the enrichment of principal elements (such as Cr, Ni, and Mn) carried by dislocation pile-ups that accumulate at boundaries.
generation.mechanism: During rapid deformation, dislocations act as vehicles that transport and pile up principal elements at the grain boundaries. This fast, non-equilibrium segregation leads to a concentration that weakens the intergranular bonds, promoting brittle cracking. This mechanism contrasts with conventional alloys, where embrittlement typically arises from slow precipitate nucleation or segregation of minor impurities.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples deformed under high strain rate/low temperature conditions will show, via atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM, a measurable increase in the concentration of principal elements at grain boundaries; these samples should exhibit intergranular, brittle fracture features and a significant drop in toughness. In contrast, the samples deformed under slower (or higher temperature) conditions will retain a uniform grain-boundary composition and display predominantly transgranular, ductile failure.
generation.baseline: The slow-deformed (or pre-homogenized) HEA sample, which exhibits uniform grain-boundary composition and maintains high toughness with transgranular fracture modes.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected under service conditions where the strain rate is high enough and temperature is low enough to prevent complete diffusion homogenization, but not so extreme as to trigger other high-temperature or cryogenic mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: While experimental evidence (e.g., from PMC11407990 and PMC6897545) supports dislocation-induced segregation under certain conditions, the exact critical concentration threshold and kinetics in a multi-component HEA remain to be precisely quantified. The current proposal extends these findings by directly linking rapid dislocation flux to toughness degradation in a single-phase material.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical single-phase HEA samples; subject one set to high strain rate deformation at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 500°C) and another set to a slower deformation protocol (or with a pretreatment that encourages homogenization). After deformation, use atom-probe tomography and high-resolution TEM to analyze the grain-boundary composition and examine fracture surfaces through SEM. Conduct parallel mechanical tests (tensile and fracture toughness) to correlate microstructural changes with ductility.
measurements: Fracture surface morphology (intergranular vs. transgranular features via SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high strain rate deformation does not result in significant grain-boundary enrichment of principal elements relative to the slow-deformed samples, or if both deformation protocols yield similar fracture modes and toughness levels, then the hypothesis that fast, dislocation-driven segregation triggers brittle behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: When the macroscopic deformation resulted in generation and movement of dislocations, the atoms of some elements easily followed the movement under the stress field generated by the slip and climb of the dislocations and accumulated as the dislocations annihilated at grain boundaries. The characteristics of multi-principal elements in RHEAs made the interaction between atoms more complex and supplied various aisles. On the other hand, the internal energy stored in the alloys by the plastic deformation increased the instability of component atoms. It indirectly promoted movement and diffusion of atoms. With the increasing temperature and decreasing strain rate, the intragranular dislocation generation was limited owing to the gradually enhanced grain boundary sliding mechanism. The dislocation movement also slowed. Meanwhile, the component element segregation disappeared. The accumulation of Ta and Mo atoms near grain boundaries not only occupied most positions of the lattices but also resulted in many intragranular atom vacancies. cited_evidence.text: Segregation of minor alloying elements to GBs often embrittles conventional alloys (, ). Grain refinement is an effective way to evade GB embrittlement because more interfaces reduce the level of individual GB segregation (). In contrast, multiple principal constitutive elements in HEAs can segregate into GBs instead of trace alloying elements. In HEAs, grain refinement can assist the segregation of principal constitutive elements to GBs and even lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases at GBs (). For example, Cr-rich bcc phases and L10-NiMn phases precipitate at GBs in nanocrystalline Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size, ~50 nm) after annealing at 450°C for only 5 min, which reduces the ductility substantially (). In addition, previous studies show that Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEAs with the grain sizes from 4.4 to 155 μm all exhibit loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures, irrespective of grain size in this range (Fig. 1). Microalloying with B in Fe-Mn steels has been reported to delay temper embrittlement at 450°C (). B can compete for GB sites and reduce GB energy and, thus, repel the embrittling element Mn due to the decreased driving force for Mn segregation

cited_evidence.text: To evade the fast segregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn into GBs, we propose to migrate the fast segregation of these elements from GBs to the preexisting precipitates that are enriched with principal embrittling elements, especially for alloys used at intermediate and high temperatures, because intermetallic compounds can deform at high temperatures, although they reduce the ductility of the alloys at room temperature compared with the single-phase alloys. On the basis of the chemical compositions of four possible GB precipitates in the Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA reported by previous studies (see table S1) (, , ), the Cr-rich σ phase absorbs Cr elements, while it repels other element segregation to GBs. Otto et al. found that GBs are rich in Ni and have no obvious segregation of embrittling elements Mn and Cr when Cr-rich σ phases were precipitated at GBs (, ). In addition, without Mn, Ni segregated in σ phase–free GBs is beneficial to GB cohesion.
